summary:
Gender identity is not criminalised in Honduras. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1899, with the age of consent set at 15 years, the same as for heterosexual sex.

The Penal Code adopted by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017 makes hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies the exercise of individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 lempiras. LGBTQ rights groups met with Congress before the code took effect to press for the wording, and both articles were retained.

The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs allows police to raid city streets, entrap sex workers under "sanitation control" and arrest anyone who "goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals". LGBTQ rights organisations have documented numerous instances in which police used this provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.

Transgender women are held in the men's prison system. At the national penitentiary in Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the "La Isla" module, located beside the unit for mentally ill prisoners; trans women are forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women, and denied conjugal visits. At the Marcala prison, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the national torture-prevention centre was she isolated from male prisoners and her feminine belongings returned. No placement-by-gender-identity policy is documented; placement follows birth sex, with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad hoc protective isolation. In October 2020 Human Rights Watch reported a Honduran judge's account of a trans woman raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, a case the judge said she had reported to prosecutors who did not investigate. The judge's conclusion was that there is no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.

Human Rights Watch's May 2009 report, "Not Worth a Penny", documented police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in Honduras. LGBTQ organisations recorded 174 violent deaths of LGBTQ people between 2009 and 2014, of whom 69 were transgender, and 264 LGBTQ people murdered between 2009 and 2017. These are raw counts; the sources give no population figure and no general homicide rate, so they establish no per-capita comparison and no ranking against other jurisdictions on risk. The specific documented killings are the shooting dead of transgender activist Cynthia Nicole on 2 January, the year not stated in the source, and the murder of trans activist Thalia Rodriguez on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa. The most recent documented killing in this record is from 10 January 2022; no later instance is documented.

Impunity is the mechanism that keeps these cases unresolved. The LAWG Education Fund report "Left in the Dark" finds that institutions fail to effectively investigate and prosecute, attributing impunity to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional mishandling of cases, and identifies obstacles to justice that fall hardest on trans women. The United States State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among the country's significant human-rights issues.

Human Rights Watch finds that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, with Guatemalan officials describing them as "not biological women". Vicky Hernandez v Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognised. A constitutional amendment of 4 May 2005 by Decree 36 restricted Articles 112 and 116 so that only a man and a woman who have that status naturally may contract marriage, banning marriage and de facto union between persons of the same sex and refusing recognition of same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other countries. Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no recognised partner status in Honduras. Following the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018, activists filed suit in the Supreme Court in May 2018 to legalise same-sex marriage; a second case was dismissed in November 2018 for technical errors, and a same-sex marriage bill presented to the National Congress on 24 May 2022 remained under discussion.
tangentialFactors:
Political hostility to LGBTQ rights is documented across the record. The two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights, only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party expressed interest in working with the LGBT community, and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats. President Juan Orlando Hernández said on 12 October 2018 that personally, as a Christian, he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop "immoral laws".

Trans visibility in public life carries a documented security cost. A trans activist and co-founder of Asociación Cozumel Trans ran for Congress for the Innovation and Unity party in Francisco Morazán at the 26 November 2017 election, receiving 11,112 votes and placing 136th for a 128-seat National Congress, an unsuccessful but potentially first openly trans candidacy. Context around that run includes Kendra Stefani Jordany's 2017 primary win, Claudia Spellman's 2012 run for the LIBRE party, and Victoria Gomez seeking asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa. In June 2013 a trans woman was granted asylum in Spain after a police officer attempted to assassinate her.

Organising has been possible but contested. Under the Constitution citizens may establish and associate with political parties and interest groups, yet initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays; the first organisations arose anyway, often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing, and were essentially ignored by the government apart from police harassment. In 2004 the government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights groups despite organised protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators, and an August 2004 church protest accompanied that recognition. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula.

The general social environment is described as one of historical discrimination against LGBTQ persons motivated by prejudice and machismo. A dated news archive for 2004 to 2011 records an LGBTI activist murdered amid violence and impunity in 2009 to 2010, extreme violence against the gay community and abuses in the post-coup period, and 2005 coverage of marriage and adoption bans, corroborating the violence timeline.

The government offers medical care to all citizens and has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, but the influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestants has made a comprehensive public programme difficult to implement. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups, and no youth-specific care or medication provisions appear in the sources.
localsOnly:
Legal name change for LGBTI persons is approved in Honduras. The sources give no procedure details, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association described the change as an "aberration in God's eyes".

Article 116 of the Constitution prohibits adoption by same-sex couples, and same-sex couples are excluded from the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.

Prison conditions for transgender residents are set out in detail by a trans activist writing in September 2017 with the national torture-prevention centre: trans women are held in the men's system, concentrated in a single module at the national penitentiary, forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women, with conjugal visits refused. At Marcala, protective isolation from male prisoners was achieved only after outside intervention. There is no placement-by-gender-identity policy.

Residents have used the courts and the ballot. The May 2018 Supreme Court suit to legalise same-sex marriage and the May 2022 congressional bill are resident-facing avenues, as is the 2017 congressional candidacy described above. Asylum grants to Honduran trans women in Spain in June 2013 and Victoria Gomez's flight to Spain after threats in Tegucigalpa concern residents rather than visitors.

Registration of LGBTQ organisations was obstructed in the 1980s and only three groups received formal recognition in 2004, after which pride marches and public organising continued, including the July 2017 march of about 400 people in San Pedro Sula.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Reuters feature on Central America's LGBT people returning HTTP 401 at research time could not be read, so its specific claims are unresolved and none are carried here.

The sources provide no entry, visa, or passport gender-marker rules for Honduras, no documentation on airport or border screening of gender-nonconforming travellers, and no sourced account of how document markers are inspected on arrival. Nothing in the inventory establishes differential treatment of trans visitors at the border.

The violence totals of 174 deaths from 2009 to 2014 and 264 from 2009 to 2017 are raw counts without denominators. No general homicide rate for Honduras appears in the inventory, so no comparison between trans or LGBTQ killings and background violence can be made from these sources, and no per-capita or comparative risk ranking is supported.

The year of Cynthia Nicole's killing on 2 January is not stated in the source inventory and has not been supplied here. The most recent dated killing in the inventory is 10 January 2022; whether later cases exist is not sourced.

No survey of transgender people in Honduras appears in the inventory, so current prevalence of discrimination or violence experienced by trans residents is unresolved. The 2009 Human Rights Watch report and the 2021 country report are dated snapshots and are presented as such.

Whether Articles 27, 321 and 321-A have been applied in any prosecuted case is not documented in the inventory; enforcement of the anti-discrimination provisions is unresolved.
